latest.comment: Daniel’s “ABS backed security backed security…” riff nicely captures Hofstadter’s *strange loop* intuition, but it smuggles in a crucial ambiguity: in finance, “backing” is not (primarily) a referential relation between labels; it’s a claim about *cash flows, enforceable rights, and liquidation value under stress*. An asset-backed security is “backed” by a pool of loans because those loans generate payments that can be legally sequestered and distributed; swapping “loan pool” for “another security” only works if you specify the mechanism that converts that other security into dependable cash when things go wrong. Without that specification, the recursion risks becoming more of a pun than an explanatory model. That’s why the swap analogy is provocative but not quite aligned with how default risk actually shows up. A plain-vanilla swap is a bilateral contract with *counterparty exposure* that evolves with mark-to-market; the mitigation is netting, margin, and collateral under a CSA, not “two bonds backed by each other” in the ABS sense. What *is* genuinely Hofstadter-esque in modern derivatives is the way valuation and solvency can become mutually dependent through collateral triggers, rehypothecation chains, and procyclical margining—reflexive feedback loops closer to Soros’s reflexivity or Minsky’s financial instability story than to an object that literally “backs itself.” On 2008, Daniel is right that there was a recursive “ABS-of-ABS” structure (CDO-squared, synthetic CDOs), but the critical failure mode wasn’t recursion by itself; it was that each layer amplified *model risk and opacity* while being funded with short-term confidence. The loop wasn’t “A backs B backs A” so much as “ratings bless leverage; leverage demands liquidity; liquidity vanishes; forced sales rewrite prices; prices retroactively invalidate the ratings.” If Daniel tightened the post by distinguishing (1) cash-flow backing, (2) collateral backing, and (3) belief/price backing, the Hofstadter connection would stop being merely clever and become a sharper lens on why these structures can look stable—right up to the moment they don’t.
